name: MatX
baseline: handwritten CUDA kernels + cuFFT (FFT pipeline); also CuPy 14.1.1 eager and NumPy 2.5.1 + SciPy 1.18.0 (Black-Scholes)
workload: 256 batched 4096-point complex FP32 FFTs with fused input normalization and calibrated-magnitude/dB post-processing (median kernel time), plus 100M FP32 Black-Scholes option prices (median time, transfers excluded).
claimed_speedup: FFT pipeline: MatX CUDAJITExecutor 0.1114 ms vs handwritten CUDA + cuFFT 0.1792 ms = 1.61x faster (MatX cudaExecutor 0.1848 ms = 0.97x, i.e. slightly slower than the handwritten version). Black-Scholes 100M FP32: MatX 16.07 ms vs CuPy 14.1.1 eager 90.32 ms = 5.62x faster, vs NumPy 2.5.1 + SciPy 1.18.0 on CPU 2965.66 ms = 184.5x faster.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA 13.0 (nvcc), MathDx 26.03 for the JIT case; FFT reproduce command: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DMATX_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON -DMATX_EN_MATHDX=ON, then ./build/examples/fft_benchmark 256 4096 2000 (CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES defaults to native). The Black-Scholes reproduce command in the README omits CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE. Host C++ compiler and version not stated.
hardware: NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10 GPU), 20-core Arm CPU (10 Cortex-X925 + 10 Cortex-A725), driver 580.159.03 (stated for the Black-Scholes run)
tradeoffs: GPU-first (NVIDIA) header-only C++20 library; the fused-kernel speedup needs the optional MathDx (cuFFTDx) backend, a supported FFT shape and the CUDAJITExecutor, and JIT compilation cost is excluded from the steady-state timing. Linux fully supported, Windows alpha. CPU executors (OpenMP, NVPL, FFTW) exist but the README gives no CPU numbers.
caveats: First-party NVIDIA numbers on one machine (DGX Spark GB10); the README says performance depends on GPU, clocks, shape and software versions. The FFT baseline is a 59-line handwritten CUDA + cuFFT pipeline written by the MatX authors (unfused normalization and post-processing kernels), and the plain cudaExecutor path is 3% slower than it, so the 1.61x comes only from JIT fusion with cuFFTDx. Tier A rests on the FFT benchmark (public examples/fft_benchmark.cu, Release build stated, CUDA 13.0, GB10 CPU/GPU named); the Black-Scholes rows alone would be tier C because the build type is not stated and MatX is timed with CUDA events in the C++ example while CuPy/NumPy are timed by examples/black_scholes_benchmark.py (separate harnesses, same equation, FP32, 100M elements, inputs and transfers excluded). The CuPy baseline is an eager expression with intermediates, not a fused CuPy kernel. No comparison against cuBLAS or other BLAS/LAPACK is published.

name: MeTA
workload: Index build time on the Blog06 and Gov2 (147 GB) web collections against Lucene and Indri; linear classification time and accuracy on 20news and Webspam against LIBLINEAR, per the ACL 2016 system-demonstration paper (numbers read from search-result summaries only).
claimed_speedup: Indexing time Blog06: MeTA 11m 23s, Lucene 20m 23s, Indri 55m 40s (about 1.8x faster than Lucene and 4.9x faster than Indri, derived from snippet data). Gov2: MeTA 1h 12m 10s, Lucene 1h 59m 42s, Indri 8h 13m 43s (about 1.7x faster than Lucene and 6.8x faster than Indri, derived from snippet data). 20news classification: MeTA 80.1% accuracy in 0.648 s vs LIBLINEAR 79.4% in 2.58 s (about 4x, derived; third-party review summary). Webspam: MeTA reaches 99.4% accuracy in 76 s while LIBLINEAR could not run for lack of memory.
tradeoffs: Index-based, out-of-core design: classification can stream data from the index (a 1.2 GB training set ran with a 128 MB resident set in the project tutorial) but the toolkit is a full framework (text analysis, retrieval, classification, topic models, parsers), so Lucene and Indri are only comparable on the retrieval/indexing part. Repo ships both LICENSE.mit and LICENSE.ncsa.
caveats: Snippet only: aclanthology.org, liner.com, preview.aclanthology.org and meta-toolkit.org were EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the paper's tables were never opened; the Blog06/Gov2 indexing figures come from a garbled table extract in a WebSearch summary and the 20news figures from a third-party review of the paper, so the verifier should re-read the PDF. Hardware, compiler, flags, library versions and query-speed results are unknown (the summary said retrieval performance across the three systems was relatively even; index sizes are comparable, Lucene 2.06 GB vs MeTA 2.84 GB on Blog06 and 11.02 GB vs 10.24 GB on Gov2). The paper is a peer-reviewed ACL 2016 demo (P16-4016), which would support tier B if the numbers are confirmed; the repo itself carries no benchmark code (website tutorials only state that LIBLINEAR is killed loading a 1.2 GB training set). Repo inactive since 2017-08-20 (last commit merges hotfix-v3.0.2); the first-party nature of the numbers and the missing methodology keep this at C.
